title: sleep
hook: drums, conches and elephants: Lanka tries to wake a sleeping giant, and he wakes up honest

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep in the Yoga Sutras: a movement of the mind, remembered in the morning as light or heavy. When someone asked how you slept, what was your one honest word? Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

Drums are pounding. Conches are blowing. People are shouting into a giant's ears, and elephants are being led over his sleeping body. Next to him, food is heaped up, ready for the moment his eyes open. It's Lanka, in Valmiki's Ramayana, and the city is under siege. Ravana needs his brother Kumbhakarna, and Kumbhakarna is asleep. Getting him up takes a crowd. Today: the sleep that isn't rest, and what a giant says when he finally wakes.
screen: `DRUMS, CONCHES, ELEPHANTS.` → `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE GIANT IS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: Kumbhakarna is Ravana's brother, a giant whom the story knows for his long sleeps. Tradition tells that his sleep came from a boon that went wrong, a wish that came out as sleep. Now the war has started without him. When he finally wakes, hungry and enormous, he eats, and he's brought to his brother. Then comes the surprise. Ravana tells him what has happened: the taking of Sita, the army at the walls. And Kumbhakarna, the sleepy one, tells the king the truth to his face. In paraphrase: you did this without listening to counsel. You acted first and thought after. Then, out of loyalty, he goes out to fight for his brother anyway, and he falls. There's more than one way into this. First, the Gita gives a name to this kind of sleep. In the fourteenth chapter, it describes tamas, the quality of darkness and heaviness, and says it binds a person through heedlessness, laziness and sleep. Sleep is on that list. Not sleep as rest, which the texts honor, but sleep as staying under, as not wanting to wake. Second, the story is fairer than a cartoon. The giant who slept through the war's beginning is the one who, once awake, speaks plainly to the king. Waking up can be an honest moment. Third, the ordinary version. A hard email. A bill. A conversation put off for months. There's a kind of Kumbhakarna sleep that has nothing to do with a bed. And one careful note: tiredness that won't lift is a matter for a doctor, never a mark of bad character. The Gita's tamas names a pull to stay under, not a diagnosis of anyone.
screen: `KUMBHAKARNA, KNOWN FOR HIS SLEEP` · `YOU ACTED WITHOUT COUNSEL` · `TAMAS BINDS THROUGH SLEEP` · `THE SLEEP THAT ISN'T ABOUT A BED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake slowly to one thing. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Let one thing come to mind that you've been sleeping through: something put off, unanswered, avoided. Don't solve it. Don't scold yourself. Just let it sit in front of you while you breathe, the way a person lies still for a moment before getting up. Then find the smallest first step, one sentence, one call, one look. Hold it lightly. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. In the Gita, one of the ways tamas binds; in the Ramayana, Kumbhakarna's long sleep, and the honest words he speaks when he wakes. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Today, wake up to one thing you've been sleeping through, and take the smallest first step: one email, one call, one honest sentence. Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's waking is told in Ramayana retellings and Ramlila performances, and Hindu teachers draw on Gita 14 to explain tamas, the quality of heaviness, as one of the three gunas.

original.note: Sanskrit tamas: darkness, heaviness, one of the three gunas. Gita 14.8 says it binds through heedlessness, laziness and sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: the giant who sleeps is just comic relief.
what it means: Kumbhakarna's sleep is the story's picture of staying under, and once awake he's the one who tells Ravana the truth.
what a scholar hears: Gita 14.8's tamas, binding through pramada, alasya and nidra, beside a character Valmiki lets speak honestly.

notes: Valmiki Yuddha Kanda: the waking of Kumbhakarna (around sarga 60 in the critical numbering; varies by edition) and his rebuke of Ravana (around sarga 63). Confirm details: drums, conches, shouting, elephants driven over him, heaped food; and the rebuke's substance (acting without counsel, doing first what should come after).
The boon of sleep (Uttara Kanda) is introduced as 'tradition tells'; popular retellings add that Saraswati turned his words. No duration given, deliberately.
Gita 14.8: 'pramada-alasya-nidrabhih' paraphrased as heedlessness, laziness and sleep.
Fairness: the lesson presents Kumbhakarna as honest and loyal, not as a figure of mockery; the science-seat line says lasting tiredness is a doctor's matter, not a character flaw.
Editor pass: 'the whole household' became 'a crowd', closer to the text; varied the stock 'turn it a few ways' lead-in.
Gita 6.16–17 (sleep in measure) was already used on day 1308 for food, so it is not repeated here.
